extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, activists, and anyone researching petitions or petitioning practices
extracted.subtask_description: A general-reference overview of what petitions are, their historical and modern uses, legal meanings (including as a pleading), and common procedural/format features such as signature requirements and online platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition is a request to do something, most commonly addressed to a government official or public entity. In the colloquial sense, a petition is a document addressed to an official and signed by numerous individuals. A petition may be oral rather than written, or may be transmitted via the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formats accepted include oral, written, and electronic submissions; petitions often rely on signatures to demonstrate support. The entry emphasizes both formal (legal) and informal (grassroots/online) senses of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition as a legal pleading
rubrics_metrics.description: In law, a 'petition' can be the title of a pleading that initiates a legal case seeking non-monetary or 'equitable' relief (e.g., a writ of mandamus, habeas corpus, custody, probate). An initial pleading seeking only money is typically called a 'complaint' in most U.S. courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'petition' terminology when the sought relief is equitable or non-monetary; examples cited include writs and habeas corpus. This distinction affects procedural posture and naming of filings in different courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on petition (summary process)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'act on petition' is a 'summary process' used in probate, ecclesiastical and divorce cases, designed to handle matters too complex for a simple motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parties exchange pleadings until a cause for a hearing is settled. Historical/disciplinary notes (Black's Law Dictionary) mention obsolete admiralty use and maritime examples in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot access petitions: signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions are commonly used in the U.S. to qualify candidates for public office to appear on a ballot; a candidate desiring printed ballot access must gather a certain number of valid signatures from registered voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature validity and meeting statutory thresholds are decisive; paid signature gatherers are a common tactic (example: 2003 California recall). After meeting signature thresholds other procedural steps (e.g., scheduling a vote) follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot initiatives and recall petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In jurisdictions allowing ballot initiatives, gathering a sufficient number of voter signatures qualifies a proposed initiative to be placed on the ballot; recall petitions similarly start eligibility for a recall election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites historic and contemporary examples (e.g., California recall) to show how petitions function procedurally to trigger electoral or initiative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online petitions as a distinct form
rubrics_metrics.description: Online petitions are a new and increasingly common form of petition; platforms (e.g., Change.org) have large user bases and enable mass signature collection via the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online petitions may differ from formal legal or ballot petitions in legal effect; the page notes their prevalence and platforms but also implies limits on legal force (see moral force entry). UK Parliament and other official petition portals are examples of institutional online petitioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitions as moral or political force (non-legal effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions can have no direct legal effect yet represent moral force and public opinion that may influence outcomes (e.g., petitions seeking Nelson Mandela's release). NGOs (such as Amnesty International) use petitions to exert moral authority on issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent legal compulsion, large-scale petitions can pressure institutions or raise public awareness. The entry frames petitions as a tool of activism and advocacy as well as a procedural instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/administrative practices for petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, petitions were handled by specific bureaucratic offices that read, copied, annotated, archived, and tracked petitions (examples: Imperial China’s Office of Transmission; Ottoman Empire bureaus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These administrative practices show institutional expectations for how petitions are received and processed (e.g., multiple copies, archiving, recording annotations and administrative actions). Useful for understanding recordkeeping and procedural channels in historical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional right to petition (U.S. First Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition Clause of the First Amendment guarantees the right of the people 'to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.' The right to petition has been held to include the right to file lawsuits against the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a protected civic and legal activity; practitioners should be aware that petitioning is constitutionally protected speech and may encompass judicial filings in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical uses and subjects of petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions are used for a variety of purposes including qualifying candidates for ballots, ballot initiatives, protests, requests for policy change, corporate personnel decisions, and appeals to moral authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides diverse examples (parliamentary petitions, NGO campaigns, corporate contexts) highlighting that content, audience, and intended effect vary; authors should tailor formality and procedural compliance to the petition’s purpose.
